figures.alt: Photo of a lighthouse on a Lake Michigan breakwater at dusk with a bright beam of light sweeping over the water.
figures.caption: A lighthouse sends a pattern of light so sailors far away can read the signal.

figures.alt: Photo of a yellow rubber duck riding gentle waves on a lake.
figures.caption: A wave moves forward, but the duck mostly moves up and down.

figures.alt: Diagram of a lamp on the left, an apple in the middle and an eye on the right. Arrow 1 goes from the lamp to the apple. Arrow 2 goes from the apple into the eye. No arrow leaves the eye. Light from the lamp bounces off the apple and enters the eye, which is how we see it.
figures.caption: We see an object when light reflects from it and enters our eyes. The eye only receives light. The apple does not make its own light.

figures.alt: Bar graph, How far a wave moved an object. Small wave 1 cm, Large wave 3 cm.
figures.caption: A small wave moved the floating object 1 cm. A large wave moved it 3 cm. Bigger waves carry more energy.

figures.alt: Bar graph, Signal accuracy at 3 meters. Flashlight code 4 out of 5, Drum code 3 out of 5.
figures.caption: Messages decoded correctly out of 5 tries: flashlight code 4, drum code 3.
